A_target.statement:
Let $\struct {R, +, \cdot}$ be a [[Definition:Ring with Unity|ring with unity]] such that:
:$\forall x \in R: x^2 = x$
Then $R$ is a [[Definition:Boolean Ring|Boolean ring]], and Boolean rings correspond exactly to [[Definition:Boolean Algebra|Boolean algebras]].

B_source.statement: A [[Definition:Commutative Ring with Unity|commutative ring with unity]] is a set $R$ with operations $+$ and $\cdot$ such that $\struct {R, +}$ is an [[Definition:Abelian Group|abelian group]], $\cdot$ is [[Definition:Associative Operation|associative]] and [[Definition:Commutative Operation|commutative]] with [[Definition:Identity Element|identity]] $1$, and $\cdot$ [[Definition:Distributive Operation|distributes]] over $+$.

substitutions.the additive inverse: each element is its own inverse, since the characteristic is two

derived.ring-theoretic notions such as ideals: filters and their complements in the algebra
derived.prime ideals of the ring: ultrafilters of the algebra, which is the basis of the representation theorem

object_map.reformulation: Reinterpret the connectives as ring operations, taking exclusive rather than inclusive disjunction as addition.

validity_conditions: Idempotence of multiplication forces characteristic two, since expanding the square of a sum gives that every element is its own additive inverse.
The dictionary is a bijection: symmetric difference and meet determine join and complement, and conversely, so the two axiomatizations describe the same objects.
Ordinary disjunction is not the ring addition, since it is not cancellative; using symmetric difference instead is what makes the transfer work.
proof_plan:
Given a [[Definition:Boolean Algebra|Boolean algebra]] $\struct {B, \vee, \wedge, \neg}$, define:
:$x + y = \paren {x \wedge \neg y} \vee \paren {\neg x \wedge y}$
:$x \cdot y = x \wedge y$
that is, [[Definition:Symmetric Difference|symmetric difference]] and [[Definition:Meet (Order Theory)|meet]].

Verify the [[Definition:Commutative Ring with Unity|commutative ring axioms]], with $0 = \bot$ and $1 = \top$.
Idempotence $x \cdot x = x \wedge x = x$ follows from [[Definition:Idempotent Operation|idempotence]] of $\wedge$.

Under this correspondence, [[Definition:Ideal of Ring|ideals]] of $R$ correspond to [[Definition:Ideal (Order Theory)|order ideals]] of $B$, and [[Definition:Prime Ideal of Ring|prime ideals]] correspond to complements of [[Definition:Ultrafilter on Set|ultrafilters]].
{{qed}}
